topic: Public International Law and Human Rights: Human Rights Framework (Universal and National)
description: This module explores the global and domestic frameworks established to protect human dignity. It covers the International Bill of Human Rights, focusing on the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (UDHR) and the two primary International Covenants, alongside India's national enforcement mechanism under the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993.

international_bill_of_human_rights.concept: The International Bill of Human Rights
key_points: Core Components: The 'International Bill of Human Rights' is an informal name given to one UN General Assembly resolution and two international treaties: The Universal Declaration of Human Rights (UDHR, 1948), the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (ICCPR, 1966), and the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights (ICESCR, 1966).

UDHR (1948): Adopted on December 10, 1948 (celebrated as Human Rights Day). It contains 30 articles. While technically a 'declaration' and initially non-binding, many of its provisions have crystallized into customary international law, making them binding on all states.

ICCPR (Civil and Political Rights): Covers 'first-generation' rights like the right to life, liberty, fair trial, and freedom of speech. States are obligated to respect and ensure these rights 'immediately'.

ICESCR (Economic, Social and Cultural Rights): Covers 'second-generation' rights like the right to work, education, and an adequate standard of living. These are subject to 'progressive realization', meaning states must take steps to fulfill them to the maximum of their available resources over time.

Protection of Human Rights Act (PHRA), 1993: This Act establishes the National Human Rights Commission (NHRC) at the central level, State Human Rights Commissions (SHRCs) at the state level, and Human Rights Courts at the district level for the speedy trial of offenses.
Role of the NHRC: The NHRC acts as India's primary human rights watchdog. It can take suo motu cognizance (on its own motion) of human rights violations.

Nature of Powers: While the NHRC has the investigative powers of a civil court (e.g., summoning witnesses, demanding documents), its final judgments are inherently 'recommendatory'. It cannot directly punish offenders or award binding compensation; it can only recommend prosecution or relief to the government.

questions.question: Which historic document, adopted by the UN General Assembly on December 10, 1948, serves as a common standard of achievement for all peoples and all nations regarding human rights?

options.B: The International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (ICCPR)
options.C: The Universal Declaration of Human Rights (UDHR)

questions.explanation: The Universal Declaration of Human Rights (UDHR) was adopted on December 10, 1948. It is a milestone document in the history of human rights, setting out fundamental human rights to be universally protected for the first time.

questions.question: A developing nation signs both the ICCPR and the ICESCR. It immediately halts state censorship to comply with freedom of speech but states it will take ten years to build enough schools to guarantee the 'right to education' for every child due to budget constraints. Is this legal under the Covenants?

options.A: No, both treaties demand immediate and absolute compliance regardless of resources.
options.B: Yes, because the right to education under the ICESCR is subject to 'progressive realization' based on available resources, while freedom of speech under the ICCPR demands immediate compliance.
options.C: No, because economic rights are strictly more important than political rights.
options.D: Yes, because neither treaty is legally binding on sovereign nations.

questions.explanation: The ICCPR (Civil and Political Rights) generally requires immediate state compliance. In contrast, the ICESCR (Economic, Social, and Cultural Rights, like education and healthcare) acknowledges economic realities and allows for 'progressive realization' over time to the maximum of a state's available resources.

questions.question: After a thorough investigation, the National Human Rights Commission (NHRC) of India finds concrete evidence that a local police officer committed custodial torture. What is the maximum punitive action the NHRC can directly take against the officer?

options.A: The NHRC can sentence the police officer to up to 5 years in prison.
options.B: The NHRC can directly dismiss the officer from police service and confiscate his salary.
options.C: The NHRC can only recommend that the state government initiate prosecution or departmental action against the officer, as its powers are recommendatory.
options.D: The NHRC can impose a binding financial fine on the officer to compensate the victim.

questions.explanation: Under the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993, the NHRC is an inquiry and recommendatory body. While it has civil court powers to gather evidence, it does not have the power of a criminal court to directly sentence, dismiss, or punish an offender. It can only 'recommend' action, prosecution, or compensation to the concerned government or authority.
